        Published 
        23 November 2026 9:07pm GMT
        
    

    


						
					

					
				

				

				





  
  

	

	
	

	
	



  
  
    Labour’s benefits review will not directly address the surge in claims from people with ADHD, The Telegraph can reveal.

Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, will propose an overhaul of personal independence payments (Pip) in a report published on Tuesday.

It is understood the review will not contain any specific recommendations on tackling the increase in claims for “neurodivergent” conditions, which include ADHD and autism.

Sir Stephen is expected to say that the benefit is “no longer fit for purpose” after the number of people claiming Pip ballooned in five years from 2.7 million to 4.1 million.

More than 106,000 people receive Pip and have ADHD as their main condition, up by almost 20 per cent in a year and by 40 per cent since Labour came to power at the July 2024 election.

The Government has approved an average of 40 Pip claims a day over the past two years in which ADHD is cited as the main condition.

Political opponents said on Monday night that Labour’s failure to tackle ADHD claims means it was “not serious” about ending the “unsustainable” rise in welfare spending.

Pip is worth up to £778 a month and is meant to help people with disabilities or long-term sickness cover extra costs such as adaptations to their homes.

The handout can be claimed by people in work as well as the unemployed and, unlike other benefits such as Universal Credit, it is not means-tested.

The Telegraph reported last week that private clinics are providing ADHD diagnoses after a one-hour appointment which costs around £795 and can enable a patient to lifelong access to benefits.

In his landmark review of worklessness last week, Alan Milburn, the former health secretary, warned of a “cash for diagnosis” culture and called for a crackdown on clinics diagnosing almost everyone they assessed with ADHD.

Robert Jenrick, Reform’s Treasury spokesman, told The Telegraph: “Mild mental health conditions like ADHD shouldn’t consign people to a life on benefits.

“Unless Timms’ review tackles the root source of the increase, the benefits bill will only keep climbing, and more human potential will be lost and wasted.”

He accused Labour of blowing “a golden opportunity” to get welfare spending down, warning “we simply cannot afford to continue with the status quo”.

The welfare bill has spiralled in recent years, with Pip spending soaring from £15bn in 2021-22 to £32bn this financial year. It is expected to hit £45bn in 2030-31.

By contrast, the entire defence budget is forecast to be only £79bn at the end of the decade.

Helen Whately, the shadow welfare secretary, said: “It’s absurd that Timms appears to ignore the extraordinary growth in claims for neurodivergent conditions like ADHD.

“Labour are not serious about fixing our broken welfare system. To make Pip fair and fit for purpose, we need to overhaul it, not just tinker around the edges.

“But the Timms Review looks set to be a damp squib as ministers once again duck the tough decisions and fail to make any savings.”

Sir Stephen’s review, which has been written with disability charities, is also expected to recommend that recipients of Pip are not required to take up health or employment support to carry on receiving their payments.

It is set to say that whilst such support, which could include mental health therapies or work experience opportunities, should be more widely offered to people claiming the handout, choosing to accept it should remain voluntary.

The report will say that cash payments should be better matched to the additional costs claimants face, meaning some people who are receiving the benefit for milder mental health conditions or back pain could see their amounts cut.

But it will also recommend making the process of applying for Pip less burdensome, after disabled people criticised it as “dehumanising”.

Last week the Institute for Fiscal Studies, the think tank, warned that doing so would lead to a flood of new applicants, saying there was “strong empirical evidence that when it is easier to apply for a benefit, more people will apply”.

A spokesman for the Department for Work and Pensions said: “The Timms review interim report made clear that Pip is no longer fit for purpose.

“When the final report is published, we will consider the recommendations alongside the Milburn review.”
